summaries.example: Imagine listening to a song. You can count its beats, but the song is more than a list of beats. The sounds blend, change, and affect one another as the song continues. Bergson used this kind of idea to explain duration: lived time is a flowing experience, not just separate points on a clock.
summaries.summary: Henri Bergson was a French philosopher whose work focused on time, change, memory, life, and freedom. He argued that the time we live through is not simply a row of identical pieces. He called this flowing, changing experience duration. In duration, feelings and memories overlap, so each moment is different from earlier moments. Bergson called this a qualitative multiplicity: many different parts held together in a living flow. He contrasted it with a quantitative multiplicity, where separate things are counted, like sheep in a field. Bergson’s method of intuition asks us to make an effort to understand something from within. He thought ordinary intelligence is useful for practical jobs, but it often breaks the world into separate, fixed pieces. Intuition tries to follow movement and change. Bergson also studied perception and memory. Perception selects what matters for action, while memory can preserve more of the past than we notice. In his account of evolution, life is creative: it continues through a shared impulse but branches into different forms. In morality and religion, he distinguished closed systems that protect a particular group from open forms that include everyone and aim at peace. Later thinkers, especially Gilles Deleuze, renewed interest in Bergson’s idea of multiplicity.
key_ideas: Bergson said lived time is different from clock time. Clock time lets us count separate units; duration is a changing flow.
He distinguished a quantitative multiplicity, such as a flock counted as numbers, from a qualitative multiplicity, such as feelings blending over time.
He thought intuition could help us understand life and experience more deeply than ordinary, practical analysis alone.
He described two kinds of memory: habit-memory, which helps us perform learned actions, and pure memory, which preserves personal experiences.
Bergson connected life with creativity and described morality as having a closed form focused on group safety and an open form reaching toward everyone.
summaries.why_it_matters: Bergson gives us a way to notice parts of life that numbers and simple labels can miss: growing older, remembering, changing our minds, creating art, and caring for others. His ideas also raise questions about whether communities should focus only on protecting their own members or should become open to everyone. Later philosophers used his account of multiplicity to rethink change and community.

important_terms.definition: Bergson’s name for lived time: a flowing experience in which past moments remain part of the present.
A group with different parts that still belong together and affect one another.
A way of understanding something by trying to experience it from within, rather than only observing it from outside.
The way earlier experiences remain with us and shape what we experience now.
The idea that life can produce genuinely new forms instead of merely repeating what was already there.

questions_to_think_about: Is a happy day just a number of minutes, or does the way the moments connect matter too?
When you remember a past event, do you experience exactly the same thing, or something changed by the present?
Can counting and measuring tell us everything important about an experience?
What might make a group welcoming to people outside it?

summaries.example: Suppose a student gives a speech after months of preparation. A purely quantitative description might list the minutes practiced, words spoken, and points made. Bergson would say this misses the student’s duration: earlier doubts, memories, effort, and confidence are carried into the present performance. The speech is not just a sum of separate states; it is a continuous, changing development.
summaries.summary: Henri Bergson’s philosophy is organized around the problem of how continuity and difference can coexist. His most enduring contribution, according to the entry, is the concept of multiplicity. A quantitative multiplicity separates items in homogeneous space so that they can be counted. A qualitative multiplicity, by contrast, is a temporal unity in which different states interpenetrate and continually develop. Bergson calls this lived temporal flow duration. Because duration conserves the past while producing something new in each moment, it supports his account of freedom: free action is not an uncaused event but the mobile expression of a developing self, unlike a mechanically determined sequence of juxtaposed states. Bergson’s method of intuition is meant to grasp duration from within. He contrasts it with intelligence, whose analytic and practical orientation divides the world according to bodily needs. Intuition is an effortful, integral experience that begins from a partial duration and expands toward related durations; thus its claim to absoluteness concerns the whole to which parts are related, not an effortless possession of every aspect at once. In Matter and Memory, Bergson treats matter and spirit as both real while trying to overcome the usual dualist opposition. Perception selects from material images what is useful for action, whereas pure memory preserves the past and can become action-guiding through movement toward the present. Creative Evolution extends these ideas to life. Bergson rejects mechanism and strict finalism, proposing a creative vital movement that remains continuous while branching into diverse forms, especially the tendencies of instinct and intelligence. key_ideas: Bergson’s central concept, qualitative multiplicity, attempts to unite heterogeneity and continuity: parts remain different without becoming externally separated.
Duration grounds Bergson’s account of freedom. Since conscious states interpenetrate rather than stand as mechanically juxtaposed causes, action can emerge as a mobile development of the self.
Intuition is not a sudden guess. It is a method involving effort, a reversal of habitual practical intelligence, and a progressive differentiation of a living continuity.
In Matter and Memory, Bergson presents perception as a selection from material images made according to bodily interests. Memory, by contrast, preserves the past and can move toward action.
In Creative Evolution, Bergson rejects both strict mechanism and traditional finalism as accounts of life. He proposes a creative vital movement whose divergence produces different forms.

The Two Sources of Morality and Religion distinguishes closed morality and static religion, which secure social cohesion, from open morality and dynamic religion, which express creativity, love, universality, and peace.
summaries.why_it_matters: Bergson’s distinctions help explain why lived experience cannot always be captured by measurement, fixed categories, or isolated snapshots. They also connect theories of time and memory with freedom, biology, knowledge, ethics, and community. His account remains philosophically important partly because later thinkers, especially Deleuze, used multiplicity to reconsider becoming and the possibility of an open community. The entry also presents Bergson’s views as positions to examine, not settled conclusions.

important_terms.definition: Lived time as an indivisible, qualitative flow in which the past is conserved and each present moment differs from earlier ones.
A multiplicity whose elements differ qualitatively yet interpenetrate within a continuous temporal movement.
A multiplicity organized by separable positions and common units, allowing things to be counted in homogeneous space.
Bergson’s disciplined effort to enter into a thing’s movement or duration, rather than reconstructing it only through external analysis.
The practical, analytic mode of intelligence that divides and organizes things for use, often treating change as a series of fixed states.
The distinction between automatic learned action and the unconscious survival of personal experiences from the past.
Bergson’s account of life as a creative movement that remains continuous while producing divergent forms and species.
The contrast between morality serving a particular society and a creative, universal morality directed toward an open society.

questions_to_think_about: Does describing a decision as a chain of separate causes leave out the way a person’s whole past shapes the decision?
Can intuition provide knowledge, or does knowledge require the kind of analysis Bergson criticizes?
How does Bergson’s distinction between pure perception and memory challenge a simple opposition between mind and matter?
If intelligence is practical and spatializing, can science still reach part of reality according to Bergson?
Can a moral rule be genuinely universal if it developed from the needs of one society?

summaries.example: Think about learning to play a difficult song on an instrument. At first, you repeat finger movements until they become automatic; this is like habit-memory. But when you perform the song, you also bring feelings, earlier mistakes, and the meaning of the music into the present. The performance is not just a pile of separate practice sessions. It is a changing whole, which helps illustrate duration and qualitative multiplicity.
summaries.summary: Henri Bergson was a major French philosopher whose ideas examine how people experience time, remember, perceive, act, and live together. His key idea is that there are different kinds of multiplicity. A quantitative multiplicity is made from separate items that can be counted, like sheep standing in different places. A qualitative multiplicity is a changing whole made from different experiences that overlap and affect each other. Bergson calls the time of such a whole duration. Duration is not like a clock face with identical units. The past remains within the present, so no two moments of a conscious life are exactly alike. Bergson connects duration with freedom because a person’s action can grow out of this moving, developing self rather than being treated as a fixed mechanical result. To understand duration, Bergson recommends intuition. This does not mean a random hunch. It means making an effort to understand something from within its movement. He contrasts intuition with intelligence, which is excellent for practical tasks because it divides and measures things, but may miss the continuous character of life. In Matter and Memory, Bergson says that perception selects from the world what is important for our bodies and actions. He separates habit-memory, which helps us repeat learned behavior, from pure memory, in which personal experiences survive, often unconsciously. In Creative Evolution, he argues that life is creative rather than simply mechanical or aimed at a completely predetermined goal. A shared vital movement produces different branches, including instinct and human intelligence. key_ideas: Bergson thought people often confuse space-like clock time with duration, the flowing time of consciousness.
A flock of sheep illustrates quantitative multiplicity because the sheep can be separated and counted. Feelings that blend into one another illustrate qualitative multiplicity.
Bergson’s intuition is a careful effort to understand movement and experience from within. It is different from simply collecting facts from outside.
Perception focuses on what matters for bodily action. Memory can preserve a richer past, and the past changes how the present is experienced.
Bergson described evolution as both continuous and creative: living things share a deep movement, yet life branches into different directions.
He distinguished closed morality, which supports the survival of a particular society, from open morality, which reaches toward universal inclusion and peace.
summaries.why_it_matters: Bergson’s philosophy encourages us to look carefully at change, memory, and human experience instead of assuming that everything can be understood as separate objects or fixed moments. It also connects personal life with larger questions about evolution, science, morality, religion, and community. His ideas later influenced philosophers who used multiplicity to think about difference, becoming, and more open forms of collective life.

important_terms.definition: Time as it is lived: a continuous flow in which earlier experiences remain active and each new moment changes the whole.
A whole made of different parts that blend and develop together instead of simply sitting side by side.
A collection whose separate parts can be placed, compared, and counted, such as objects in different locations.
A method of understanding that tries to enter into an experience or process instead of looking at it only from the outside.
A practical way of thinking that analyzes, separates, and organizes things so we can use them to meet our needs.
Memory for learned actions, contrasted with the continuing, usually unconscious preservation of personal experiences.
Bergson’s theory that life changes creatively through a common impulse that branches into different forms.
A morality that protects one group, contrasted with an open morality that aims to include all people.

questions_to_think_about: What is lost when a changing experience is described only with numbers?
Why might Bergson say that remembering is not the same as replaying an old event exactly?

Should moral rules mainly protect one community, or should they apply to everyone?
